INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
The Annunciation Light Alliance (“Alliance”) is a
non-partisan, parent-led advocacy group that formed
following the mass shooting at Annunciation Catholic
Church in Minneapolis, Minnesota on August 27,
2025. Hundreds of Annunciation School students,
teachers, staff, parents, and parishioners were attending the first all-school mass of the new academic
year when a shooter, who after extensive research selected an AR-15 semi-automatic rifle in order to inflict
maximal harm, fired 116 rounds through the stainedglass windows of the church  in under three minutes.
Two students, ten-year-old Harper Moyski and eightyear-old Fletcher Merkel, were killed, and dozens of
others were injured.
The Alliance seeks to foster a sense of shared responsibility and thoughtful action alongside policymakers, educators, faith leaders, and community
partners to help ensure all Minnesota children can
learn, play, and worship in safe environments free
from gun violence. The Alliance values and promotes
the principles of Catholic social teaching—themes
that guide Catholics to create a just world. These
themes of solidarity, family, responsibility, stewardship, and the sanctity of human life reside at the core
of Catholic education and practice. They illustrate

1 Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, counsel for amicus

2

that the proliferation of a ssault weapons is antithetical to the livelihood of the Annunciation community.
INTRODUCTION AND
 SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
On August 27, 2025, hundre ds of members of the
Annunciation Catholic Church and School community—including every first- through eighth- grade
student—gathered for a morning of worship in the
first all-school mass of the new academic year. 2
Shortly after the service began, an individual approached the side of the church armed with a 17DM-
15 AR-15 rifle, a 12-gauge shotgun, and a 9-millimeter pistol. See Deena Winter & Paul Walsh, Suspected
Shooter Legally Purchased Rifle, Pistol and Shotgun;
Local Politicians Call for Action. 3 The shooter obtained all three weapons lawfully. Id. The individual
fired 116 rounds through the church’s stained-glass
windows in under three minutes. More than 300 students, each exercising their First Amendment right to
worship, quickly went from singing hymns to sheltering under the church’s wo oden pews. Two students
were murdered, dozens of people live with lifelong
physical injuries, and hundreds continue to struggle
with the mental toll of the shooting.

2 Unless otherwise noted, accounts of the August 27, 2025
mass shooting and its aftermath draw on interviews of Annunciation community members conducted between September 24,
2026, and October 6, 2026, by members of the University of Minnesota Law School Gun Violence Prevention Clinic. Interview
transcripts are on file with the Clinic.
3 https://www.startribune.com/minnesota-church-shooterguns-permits/601462465.

3

Later that same day, Petitioner Cutberto Viramontes filed the petition for a writ of certiorari asking this Court to ensure continued widespread public
access to the same type of weapon the attacker used
to terrorize Annunciation.
The assailant’s journal, discovered after the attack, reveals the centrality of the AR-15 to the
shooter’s planned objectives. 4 The journal demonstrates that the attacker’s goal was to perpetrate grotesque violence and inflict the maximum amount of
harm.5 And it shows that the shooter carefully researched available options and selected the AR-15 because of its unique capacity to achieve these goals.6
This Court has recognized that “dangerous and
unusual weapons” may lawfully be regulated “consistent with the Nation’s hi storical tradition of firearm regulation.” N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v.
Bruen, 597 U.S. 1, 24 (2022). The Annunciation community’s experience is a stark and recent illustration
of how dangerous and unusual a weapon the AR-15 is.
The AR-15 and similar assault weapons 7 inflict catastrophic injuries that were unimaginable at the
Founding. They can fire hundreds of rounds in seconds and are accurate at long distances. Rounds shot
from AR-15s deliver so much force that even graze

4 See Translated Journal of Annunciation Shooter (“Translated Journal”). On file with the undersigned counsel of record.
5 Translated Journal, Book 1, at 15 (June 26, 2025).
6 Id.
7 “Assault weapons” is the term used in the challenged statutes. See Cook County Ordinance No. 93-O-37; 1993 Conn. Pub.
Acts 93-306. Amicus uses it here solely for consistency with the
record.

4

wounds can cause traumatic brain injuries, explode
internal organs, and cause other serious, long-term
injuries that, even if survived, lead to lifelong disabilities and medical complications. See infra p. 20. And
these weapons’ capacity for mass violence causes
uniquely devastating complications for medical providers and first responders. See infra pp. 21-23. This
is no surprise, as these weapons derive from military
weapons built to kill effectively and efficiently.
The destructive features of assault weapons also
render ineffective the best school-security procedures.
Annunciation took every precaution and employed
best practices to protect its students and community.
Prior to the shooting, it invested hundreds of thousands of dollars to retrofit its school and church with
state-of-the-art security measures and received an
“A+” security review from a consultant from the U.S.
Department of Homeland Security. But because the
shooter had access to an AR-15, none of those
measures proved to be enough.
Regulating assault weapons is also consistent with
our national historical tradition of regulating firearms to protect the rights of others. Included in the
First Amendment’s guarantee of free exercise of religion for each individual is “a correlative freedom to
engage in group effort toward those ends.” Roberts v.
U.S. Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609, 622 (1984); see Roman
Cath. Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo , 592 U.S. 14, 19
(2020) (per curiam). The Annunciation community’s
story shows that the proliferation of assault weapons,
and the mass violence they uniquely facilitate, frustrates the ability of Catholics and other people of faith

5

to gather, worship in community, and exercise religion without fear. After the shooting, some Annunciation survivors will no longer attend mass, not only at
Annunciation, but at any church.
The proliferation of assault weapons is antithetical to Catholic social teaching and infringes on Annunciation community members’ ability to live consistent with foundational Catholic principles. This
brief shares the story of the Annunciation community—a tragic story that shows all too graphically why
assault weapons are dangerous and unusual tools
that burden the exercise of Annunciation members’
Catholic faith, despite their diligence before the attack and their resilience in its aftermath. Amicus
urges the Court to affirm the judgments below.
ARGUMENT
I. The Shooter’s Access To  An AR-15 Enabled
Them To Inflict Uniquely Devastating Harm
On The Annunciation Catholic School Community.
The Annunciation Catholic Church and School
form the center of a vibrant Catholic community in
southwest Minneapolis. The church’s sign, large and
visible, appears at the end of an oak-lined street, just
blocks away from several Annunciation family homes.
Many Annunciation parents and their children live
only a few minutes from school and church, making
school dropoff convenient on most mornings.
Today, children play while cars line up for parent
pick-up. Boys serving as crossing guards jostle each
other and shout to their supervisor, “Are we done yet?

6

Can we go?” The Principal greets kids and parents individually by name. On Fridays, school uniforms are
not required, but many kids wear Annunciationbranded t-shirts or hoodies. Emblazoned across clothing is the school’s unofficial motto for the year, “Move
your feet.”8 Alongside these words, the initials “FM”
and “HM” appear on the sleeves. Other shirts and
bracelets say “Harper,” “Fletcher,” or both.
Inside the school, “20 + C + M + B + 26” is written
in chalk on every door, marking the date in accordance with the annual Catholic tradition of “chalking
the door” as a prayer for Christ’s blessing and protection. The school has engaged in this practice for decades, but the protection it implores carries more
weight now than ever before.
To ensure the physical protection of the school, Annunciation underwent a security upgrade between
2023 and 2025. A consultant from the Department of
Homeland Security advised the school on appropriate
measures to keep the students, staff, and faculty safe
and awarded the school an “A+” after concluding his
security review. Doors were tinted, security cameras
installed, windows updated, access keys changed. The
school spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to provide a safe space for community worship and education.
On the day before the attack, the second day of
school, the entire school walked over to the church,

8 The Annunciation Principal noted that “move your feet” is
the latter half of an African proverb, “When you pray, move your
feet.” This proverb connects to a biblical passage from Luke 1:79,
“Guide our feet into the way of peace.”

7

sat in the pews, and talked about what it means to “be
safe at school.” Children were reminded to listen to
adults, follow directions, and “help your buddies.”
On August 27, 2025, Annunciation’s security system and administrative practices functioned exactly
as intended. The shooting happened anyway.
* * *
A single gunshot rang out first. The Annunciation
Principal thought to himself, “Could that be a firecracker just outside the wi ndow?” Then there were
two more. The noise was outs ide the left side of the
church. Someone voiced the same thought aloud, “Is
that a firework?” Then the cracks began coming rapidly, and their real source became clear. Multiple people shouted, “Everyone get down!” The deacon at the
front of the sanctuary yelled it into his microphone,
“Get down!”
The Principal stood up and moved toward the side
of the sanctuary, where bullets were flying into the
church. He walked out the fi rst set of doors, his first
instinct to confront the shooter, but stopped before the
set of doors leading outside the church. Guided by the
Holy Spirit’s presence, he thought, “If I leave, who will
stay with the kids?”
He came back inside and stood with his back to the
stone wall of the church, fa cing the sanctuary of students cowering under pews. He moved window to window, parallelling the steps of the shooter outside. Bullets exploded through the narrow stained-glass windows, whizzing by him and into the church full of children, teachers, and parishioners.

8

The children sought refuge under the thick and
ancient wooden pews, many laying on top of one another as shields. Teachers held children’s hands and
prayed. Parents who had been attending mass went
to every single door and held them shut, ready to confront anyone who attempted to enter.
Two students were not able to take cover underneath the pews. When the shooting moved toward the
back of the sanctuary, the Principal went to them.
Knowing in that moment that they were gone, he sat
with Harper and Fletcher and offered his care while
simultaneously trying to protect the other children
from seeing them. He lo oked from Harper and
Fletcher to the kids sheltering around them, who
were staring at him, wide-eyed, asking, “Are we going
to be ok?”
Multiple adults called 911 from within the church.
The first officer to respond arrived in minutes. By the
time he arrived, the shooting had stopped. He entered
the sanctuary and said to the people who were still
sheltering inside, “For everyone who is able, it is time
to get up and leave now.”
Older children, bleeding from shrapnel wounds,
shepherded first-graders out from underneath shards
of wood and the remnants of pews, saying, “Come on,
it’s time to go, it’s ok.”
Annunciation Catholic Church has fourteen small
reliefs on the walls of th e nave. These represent the
fourteen stations of the cro ss, and they depict Jesus
Christ on the day of his crucifixion. Commonly, the
stations of the cross will be arranged along a path,
along which worshippers move in order, stopping to

9

say prayers associated with each station. Harper and
Fletcher were sitting between stations twelve and
thirteen. Station twelve depicts Jesus dying on the
cross, and station thirteen is Jesus’s Mother, Mary,
holding him after he had died. Although these children did not have their parents with them in those
moments, they had a Father, and they had a Mother.
* * *
Two blocks away, an Annunciation parent was
walking his dog when he heard what he at first
thought was a roofer’s na il gun. He asked a woman
walking by, “That sounds like gunshots, right?” “Yes,”
she answered, “It sounds like it’s coming from the
school.”
When the alert for a “pediatric mass casualty”
sounded over the loudspeaker that morning, one general trauma surgeon had already been at the hospital
for over 24 hours. She had just treated five casualties
from an unrelated mass shooting the night before.
Alongside her colleagues, she initiated the hospital’s
mass casualty protocols and prepared operating
rooms before the first ambulances arrived.
Parents rushed to the school grounds. Shortly after the shooting stopped, one mother was told that her
child might be one of the critically injured children.
But the damage caused by the AR-15 was so severe
that the child was unrecognizable. The mother simply
could not tell whether it was her child or someone
else’s. The mother and her husband held the child on
the grass outside of the church as they waited for an
ambulance and told the ch ild how much they were
loved. The ambulance arrived, but only one parent

10

was able to ride along. As the ambulance arrived, the
mother noticed the child’s shoes were not the ones her
child had worn that day. The child’s father was only
able to confirm that their child was not the one taken
away in the ambulance when he reunited with their
uninjured child in the school gym later on. He says it
felt like seeing a ghost.
Upon arriving at the school, one parent encountered an injured woman lying on the ground outside.
She had been shot in the leg. The woman’s face had
turned white and pale. When the parent asked if he
could do anything for her, she just shrugged as if to
say, “I don’t know what you should do.”
An emergency care doctor who lives in the Annunciation neighborhood was the first physician to arrive
after the attack. He immediately began assisting with
triage, ambulance coordination, and the difficult process of reuniting parents with their children in the
school gym. With children in shock and wearing identical uniforms, and attendance sheets incomplete because it was so early in the morning, responders
struggled to account for each child.
One mother was on the bus on the way to the Minnesota State Fair when people started murmuring
around her. She heard sirens; ambulances began
passing the bus. “There mu st be a crash ahead,” she
thought. Then someone said, “there was another
shooting,” with a resigned shake of the head. Each
message brought the shooting closer to her family. A
school shooting. A school shooting in southwest Minneapolis. A message from a parents’ group chat:
“Shooting at mass this morning.” Then she got a call
from a paramedic. “I am an EMT and I have your son

11

here with me; he was shot in the arm; his vitals are
stable; we are on the way to the hospital.”
Back at the school, the uniforms of state patrol officers created a “sea of maroon” as parents and first
responders congregated in the back parking lot of the
school. Children who were not awaiting medical attention outside had been us hered into the school’s
gym and cafeteria for reunification.
One child, in shock, reported to first responders
that she had not been shot. She was bleeding, but she
said that she had fallen and hit her head. While treating her, first responders found that she had been
grazed by a bullet. The bu llet exerted so much force
that it caused a life-threatening brain bleed. Its energy alone passing by her head caused “blast effect
damage.” After rushing her into surgery, doctors removed a portion of her skull, placed her head in a helmet, and were only later able to surgically reattach
the removed piece. Somehow, she survived.
The rapid, near-perfect first response and the coincidental proximity of two Level 1 trauma centers to
the church fundamentally changed the outcome of the
shooting. Police blocked highway entrance ramps so
ambulances could get to hospitals unobstructed. Ambulance crews enacted the transportation protocols
that emergency drills had prepared them to employ.
Some injured children were able to get to the operating room in under an hour, a virtually unheard-of
swiftness.
When the injured children arrived at the hospital,
many of them were confused and screaming, terrified
that the attacker was still coming after them. In the

12

hours after, doctors fielded calls from panicked parents trying to determine where their children were
and whether they were alright. The hospital staff
struggled to give parents any meaningful information
because many of the children were either unrecognizable, already in surgery, or too traumatized to even
provide their names.
Contrary to some stories, the stained-glass windows of the church did not shatter. They were punctured with neat holes. The shooter’s AR-15 shot bullets designed to explode after their first impact. After
efficiently piercing the windows, the bullets fragmented, launching shrapnel in every direction. Today, many children still have pieces of lead in their
bodies. Some will carry the shrapnel for the rest of
their lives.
One family had an injured child being treated at a
local hospital. The child’s sister, who had also been in
the church, refused to go into the hospital hallways in
her uniform because she was scared that people would
know she had been at Annunciation. Her mom helped
her change in the hospital bathroom, where she wiped
other children’s blood off of her daughter’s new sneakers.
First responders struggled to identify which children were killed in the shooting because of the unusual destructiveness of the AR-15. Harper Moyski’s
parents decided to split up, with one at the hospital in
case she was there, and one at the school. When first
responders had accounted for every child except two,
the doctor at the school and law enforcement had to
notify the parents. The Moyskis had to learn their

13

child had been murdered while separated from each
other.
A few months after the attack, more of Harper’s
remains would be found inside the church. See
Michelle Krupa, The Shooting Finally Stopped. Then
Came Everything Else, CNN (May 17, 2026).9 Because
of the violence wrought by the AR-15, her family had
to cremate their daughter twice.
* * *
After the shooting, no one was required to return
to school until the community had celebrated the lives
of Harper and Fletcher. Ha rper was an aspiring veterinarian; she wanted to visit every U.S. national
park; she loved turtles. Fletcher was in a band with
his friends; he loved fishing and playing with Legos.
Fletcher’s best friend keep s the last Lego set they
built together displayed in his room. The school has
placed their desks, which in Annunciation tradition
typically follow children from classroom to classroom,
first through eighth grade, in a hallway that people
can choose to visit. There is a basket and notepad on
each desk for children to wr ite letters and prayers to
their friends.
Many teachers did not believe that anyone would
be able to return to school. At an initial meeting, Dr.
David Schonfeld, an expert who has counseled communities after school shootings since Columbine, provided guidance. He said, “No one believes there’s a

9 https://www.cnn.com/interact ive/2026/05/us/minneapolisannunciation-school-shooting-recovery/.

14

time to come back. If you’re waiting to feel ready, you
won’t.”
In the end, nearly every living student came back
to Annunciation to learn, and every single teacher
came back to school to teach.
* * *
Even though the shooting stopped, the costs—
physical, emotional, spirit ual, financial—have and
will not. Children now have extremely different needs
at school. Some kids are na vigating the loss of a sibling or a best friend. Some have formal PTSD diagnoses. Many have regular medical appointments to deal
with ongoing physical and mental effects of the shooting. A grim appointment with a doctor “to get lead levels checked” is not an unus ual part of an Annunciation family’s schedule.
In order to anticipate sensory triggers, some teachers check the weather more often and plan activities
around whether there is going to be a thunderstorm.
Others build more flexibility into their lesson plans
and practice re-engaging a classroom after once-ordinary noises like sirens and construction disrupt focus.
Counting students over and over again to make sure
all are safely accounted for has become a compulsive
habit. See Krupa, supra.
At six years old, one Annunciation student became
one of the youngest injured survivors of a school
shooting in American history. He did not know what
a bullet was before the attack. The child suffered a
nearly fatal laceration of his spleen. The significant
amount of retained shrapnel found “head to toe” in his
small body created elevated lead levels, which can

15

compromise learning and behavior in children. For
months after the attack, the child’s parents found
fragments of lead in his bed as his body naturally
“shed” what shrapnel it could. Bullets from the
shooter’s AR-15 are now splinters of lead embedded
along this child’s left side that, in his words, “light up
like Christmas lights” on medical scans.
Since the shooting, Annunciation has spent more
than a million dollars on additional security, despite
already having an “A+” school safety rating from U.S.
Department of Homeland Security. The middle school
windows were upgraded because teachers did not feel
safe in the ground-level classrooms. For several
months, the school employed 24-hour security guards.
Today, a security guard is present whenever children
are in the building.
As the school year continued, Annunciation carpeted the school’s tile floor s to soften the clang from
falling metal water bottles. Despite this and other efforts to make the school less sensory stimulating,
teachers noticed for months that the sound of a chip
bag popping would send kids ducking under lunch tables.
Though the community has returned to school,
they have not returned to church in the same way.
Weekly mass is now held in  the auditorium, and services have been re-oriented to feel different from those
previously held in the sanctuary next door. There are
certain songs they still cannot sing; the congregation
faces a different direction so that there are no windows to the left of where people are sitting.

16

The Annunciation Principal remembers that, during Fletcher’s funeral, held in a church, the beginning
of a hymn that had played during mass on August 27
caused children to drop under the pews.
Many families have not been able to attend Catholic mass at any church on Sundays. “I have lost religion,” relayed one parent.
Annunciation instructs children on the themes of
Catholic social teaching, which honor the sanctity of
life, the power of community, and the need to address
structural injustice to support the common good.
Alongside these themes, children learn about the
practical actions associated with them—corporal and
spiritual Works of Mercy. The Annunciation Principal
reflects that it used to be hard to teach children what
“Works of Mercy” means. To day, he remembers that
despite not knowing whether the shooting was over,
people paused with Harper and Fletcher. They held
their hands, kissed their foreheads, and prayed over
them. An adult covered their faces with cloths. No one
has to explain Works of Mercy anymore. Every student present in that church knows what it means to
minister to the wounded, comfort the afflicted, hold
the hand of the dying, and bury the dead.
* * *
In their actions before, during, and in the year
since the attack on Annunc iation Catholic Church,
the Annunciation community has consistently and
firmly lived by the tenet, “love one another as I have
loved you.” Students, teachers, and parishioners protected each other on August 27. Today, the Alliance

17

seeks to protect everyone from the same violence, profound loss, and hardship its community has experienced.
One parent wants to be able to tell his two children
that leaders have made the necessary changes to ensure that the chances of a mass shooting taking place
in any school are “very, very small.” His son had been
best friends with Fletcher. One night, the parent went
to get his son ready for bed and found him praying. “I
am asking God to bring Fletcher back,” the young boy
stated, as if it were any other prayer.
Another parent recognizes that there are children
in our country today not yet personally touched by
gun violence whom we might still be able to protect.
She shares, “I can only assume that most people, like
me, think that they are safe. And they aren’t. . . . It’s
like we’re all riding down the highway without a seatbelt on.”
Community members shared how painful it can be
to hear their story reduced to two children dead and
twenty-seven injured. Interviewees shared how the
shooting has placed stress on marriages, caused parents to take leave from work, and robbed families of
the children they had before, and the children they
could have become. For many Annunciation families,
what happened on August 27 has “completely taken
over [their] lives” and “this is [their] forever now.” As
one parent shared, “I often think about the fact that
while I’m living my ‘after,’ this is still someone else’s
‘before.’ I would do anything  in my power to go back
to my ‘before’ but the best I have is trying to protect
someone else’s.”

18

To those who were not there that day in August, a
reminder from the Principal of Annunciation Catholic
School: “Blessed are the Peacemakers, called to lead
the way.”
II. Assault Weapons Inflict Catastrophic Injuries That The Founders Could Not Have Anticipated.
The Annunciation community’s story demonstrates the disconnect between our nation’s historical
use and understanding of firearms and the unique,
historically unprecedented devastation that modern
assault weapons can inflict.
A. This Court’s Precedents Authorize State
Regulation of Weapons That Cause
Harms Unknown to the Founders.
As this Court has recognized, an “important limitation on the right to keep and carry arms” is that not
all weapons receive Second Amendment protection.
District of Columbia v. Heller , 554 U.S. 570, 627
(2008). The Second Amendment does not establish “a
right to keep and carry any weapon whatsoever in any
manner whatsoever and for whatever purpose.” Id. at
626. On the contrary, this nation has a “historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous and
unusual weapons.’” Id. at 627 (citation omitted).
As developed in detail in other briefs in support of
Respondents in this case, this tradition of regulating
dangerous and unusual weapons has been observed
and reaffirmed by political commentators from the
time of the Founding, the common law, and statutes
and legal cases from the sixteenth-century through

19

the nineteenth. See Bruen, 597 U.S. at 21 (citing Heller, 554 U.S. at 627).
This Court has also explained that the Second
Amendment does not require the government to identify an exact historical analogue to a challenged regulation to demonstrate that it is consistent with the nation’s history and tradition. See United States v.
Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680, 692 (2024). Requiring otherwise would impose a functionally impossible obligation to identify a precise “historical twin” to justify
any regulation. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30. Nor does the
government have to prove that a modern regulation
addresses the exact societal problems that motivated
the Founders to enact their own types of firearm regulations. See id. at 27. “The regulatory challenges
posed by firearms today are not always the same as
those that preoccupied th e Founders in 1791 or the
Reconstruction generation in 1868.” Id. It is accordingly enough to show that the modern regulation addresses situations where firearms are being “misused
in other ways that were unknown to our forebears but
pose an equivalent risk to persons or property.” Wolford v. Lopez , 609 U.S. 185, 220 (2026) (Barrett, J.,
concurring). When a State identifies “particular
‘abuse[s]’ of the right” to keep and bear arms, “it can
respond with ‘focused regulations’ to address the
threat.” Id. (citing Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 700). This is
especially apt where the mo dern law is addressing a
societal problem or technological developments that
did not even exist at the Founding. See Bruen , 597
U.S. at 27.

B. Assault Rifles Cause Devastating Injuries.
The Annunciation community’s experience painfully illustrates how the AR-15 is a dangerous and unusual weapon that may lawfully be regulated “consistent with the Nation’s hi storical tradition of firearm regulation.” Bruen, 597 U.S. at 24.
AR-15s cause uniquely harmful injuries. A doctor
who was at the scene of the Annunciation attack explained that while surgeons can fix a bullet hole
caused by a pistol, the sheer force of AR-15 rounds can
“explode” internal organs or cause severe, irreparable
internal damage. One child who was struck inside the
church suffered a nearly fatal laceration of his spleen
and requires ongoing medical treatment more than a
year later.
Annunciation students continue to need intense
medical support to address retained lead shrapnel.
AR-15 bullets, designed to explode after first impact,
fragmented after going through the church’s stainedglass windows. Significant amounts of shrapnel were
retained in children’s small bodies, creating heightened lead levels and “shedding” of the shrapnel over
time. In one child’s body, doctors found shrapnel from
“head to toe,” fragments of  which eventually started
to naturally “shed.” His parents found bullet fragments in the six-year-old’s bed for months. Many families are now familiar with what shrapnel looks like
on their child’s medical scans. One parent shared that
her child’s doctors told her that they do not yet fully
know the long-term effects of this amount of lead
trapped in a growing child’s body.

21

Due to the physical force of this weapon, even
graze wounds from AR-15 bullets cause traumatic
brain injuries. “Blast effect damage” is understood by
medical professionals to be injuries caused by the velocity alone of an AR-15 bullet. As reported above, supra at 11-12, one child started bleeding and suffered
a life-threatening brain bleed simply because an AR-
15 bullet passed by her head. Doctors had to remove
a portion of her skull. Over a year after her injury, she
continues to need surgeries.
AR-15 injuries, even if non-fatal, cause lifetime
medical complications, disabilities, and emotional
trauma. Many children cont inue to have their elevated lead levels tested on a regular basis and receive
ongoing medical care to treat their injuries. Both children and adults have been diagnosed with PTSD and
attend trauma therapy regularly.
C. Assault Rifles Cause Unique Stress on
Medical Providers and First Responders.
The effect assault weapons have on the medical
system and healthcare providers also demonstrates
the fundamental difference between these weapons
and long guns or pistols.
Large numbers of providers are needed to treat the
injured in mass casualties, and providers and resources are drawn away from their normal day-to-day
work, delaying or derailing the treatment of other sick
patients. A responding physician pointed out that a
single critically injured trauma patient harmed by an
assault weapon, like the A nnunciation children, can

22

require the services of fifty to sixty healthcare providers in just a few hours.
One doctor continues to look back on his experience at Annunciation after subsequent shootings. He
and his colleagues have remarked how “grateful” they
are when attackers use handguns rather than assault
weapons, because the resulting number of injured
people and the extent of those injuries are comparatively minor to the kind of carnage they see after attacks like the Annunciation mass shooting.
One general trauma surgeon who responded to the
attack does not recall responding to a mass shooting
during her entire residency. In just the last year, however, she has treated patien ts from five mass shootings. The greater the frequency of mass casualty
events, with their high volumes of critically injured
patients, the less time healthcare workers have to
process, and the more they suffer from burnout and
leave their jobs.
As one doctor reported, the trauma is simply different when the victims are children. The Annunciation community has maintainted relationships with
many first responders since August 27. Community
members learned that dozens of officers took leave after the attack. The Principal shared, “More EMTs and
first responders have left their positions because of
what they experienced at Annunciation than after
any other event in Minnesota history.”
While modern medicine is capable of confronting
mass harms, there are limits to the care medical providers can offer when so many suffer so much violence
at once. In the eyes of one Annunciation parent and

23

ICU physician, medicine and the medical system
simply cannot keep up with the development of weapons like AR-15s that are designed to inflict so much
damage.
D. Assault Rifles Enable Mass Violence at
Horrific Speed and Magnify the Lethality of Gun Violence.
The uniquely devastating physical injuries that
AR-15s cause still do not capt ure the true impact of
these weapons on a community. The stories shared
here result from less than three minutes of fire from
an assault weapon. The AR-15 allowed the shooter to
enact mass violence without even entering the
church. In fact, the shooter came no closer than six
feet from the church windows. As one parent observed, an AR-15 doesn’t give anyone enough time to
run or hide.
After utilizing the AR-15 and before the shooter’s
suicide, the shooter switched to the shotgun. The difference in effects is striking. The attacker fired no
more than two shots with the shotgun, compared to
over 100 rounds from the AR-15 in a few moments.
Unlike the AR-15 bullets that pierced the stainedglass windows leaving a neat hole, the shotgun pellets
immediately shattered the glass they struck.
The amplified lethality of the AR-15 in the Annunciation attack underpins ev ery aspect of the community today.

E. No Amount of Precaution Can Prevent
the Harm Caused by Assault Weapons.
To combat the rise of gun violence and school

created a protocol to lock doors during masses. Following these security inve stments, the school was
awarded an “A+” rating for security. But because the

III. The Second Amendment Permits Legislatures To Regulate Assault Weapons To
Protect The Free Exercise Of Religion.
A shooter with an assault weapon disrupted the
Annunciation community’s ex ercise of their First
Amendment rights to freely exercise their religion
and peacefully assemble on August 27, 2025. The consequences of that tragedy reverberate today. The proliferation of assault weapons inhibits many in their
community from fully practicing their Catholic faith.
The challenged regulations are a constitutional
means of protecting the exercise of other fundamental
rights, especially rights often exercised collectively,
such as the practice of religious worship.
Legislatures have historically regulated firearms
to protect the ability of others to exercise their own
fundamental rights. See, e.g., William Baude & Robert Leider, The General-Law Right to Bear Arms , 99
Notre Dame L. Rev. 1467, 1491 (2024) (noting that,
traditionally, “the state could regulate a right for limited purposes, such as to protect the rights of others.”). Restrictions on firearms protect the exercise of
individual fundamental rights to vote, pray, speak,
and peaceably assemble. See Joseph Blocher & Reva
B. Siegel, When Guns Threaten the Public Sphere: A
New Account of Public Safety Regulation under Heller, 116 Nw. U. L. Rev. 139, 141 (2021). For example,
the common-law public disorder crimes recognized
from the sixteenth into the nineteenth centuries to
criminalize riots, routs, and other unlawful assemblies exemplify the kind of historical firearms restrictions that existed to protect the fundamental

28

right to peaceably assemble. See generally Mark Anthony Frassetto, To the Terror of the People: Public
Disorder Crimes and the Original Public Understanding of the Second Amendment , 43  S. Ill. U. L.J. 61
(2018). Historical affray laws, which prohibited carrying weapons “to the Terror of the People,” restricted
the carrying and bearing of firearms to prevent others
from experiencing terror when performing daily tasks
in public. See id. at 76-77; Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 697.
This Court’s modern Second Amendment jurisprudence also authorizes the enactment of firearms regulations to protect the exe rcise of other fundamental
rights. Heller identified bans on firearms in government buildings and schools as “presumptively lawful,” and this Court has en dorsed these “sensitive
places” laws throughout its treatment of the Second
Amendment since Heller. See, e.g., Heller, 554 U.S. at
626-27; Wolford, 609 U.S. at 193. Bruen recognized
eighteenth- and nineteenth-century laws which fully
prohibited firearms in legislative assemblies and polling places, where citizens exercise the right to vote
and peaceably assemble, and in courthouses, where
the right to due process is protected in the criminal
legal system. Bruen, 597 U.S. at 30 (“[T]hese locations
were ‘sensitive places’ where arms carrying could be
prohibited consistent with the Second Amendment.”).
Just as there are locations in which the Constitution
permits legislatures to fully prohibit arms to protect
other fundamental rights, so too does it permit the restriction of specific types of weapons that impede a
community’s ability to exercise their faith freely.
The danger assault weapons pose to public safety

29

has fundamentally altered the Annunciation community’s ability to freely practice their Catholic faith.
The ability to worship in community at mass is central to Catholic worship. The shooter’s use of an assault weapon simultaneously devastated the community while also depriving them of the place that
should have been the community’s refuge after tragedy.
The proliferation of assault weapons, and those
weapons’ devastating impact on the Annunciation
community, have prevented several members from attending church at Annunciation, or even attending
any church at all. One parent professes that she “lost
religion” on August 27, 2025. That same parent relays
that her children who were present in the church during the attack were unable to attend the funeral mass
of a beloved family member.
One family’s child wore a dress at her First Communion that four generations of her family had worn
at that milestone. The mother can no longer bring
herself to look at that dress because of the memory of
what happened in the building where it was last
worn. Her family struggles to reconcile the church as
both a sacred place and a place of tragedy. The proliferation of assault weapons in private civilian life is
also antithetical to Catholic social teaching, which
values life and honors human dignity. See Brief for
Amicus Curiae the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops in Support of Neither Party at 6 (“Amicus
. . . affirms the right of self-defense while rejecting the
premise that protection of that right disables political
communities from regulating any weapon capable of
defensive use.”).

30

First Amendment rights necessarily encompass
the right to assemble as a congregation to worship
and pray. See Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist. , 597
U.S. 507, 524 (2022) (citing Emp. Div., Dep’t of Hum.
Res. of Or. v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872, 877 (1990)) (recognizing the centrality of performing acts of faith to the
Free Exercise Clause). As Annunciation’s experience
makes plain, assault weapons interfere with the right
to assemble and freely exercise religion. The Court
should uphold the challenged regulations because
they are consistent with the historical tradition of regulating firearms to protect the fundamental rights of
others.
